lessons.title: Real Estate and Telecom: Pre-Sales, ARPU, and Capital-Heavy Models

body.text: Real estate and telecom both swallow enormous amounts of capital before they earn anything, but they hide it in opposite ways. A developer sells flats years before the revenue appears in its profit and loss statement. A telecom operator books revenue every month while spending thousands of crores on a network whose payoff arrives much later. In both, the reported P&L is the last place to look.

children.text: DLF, Macrotech Developers, Godrej Properties, Oberoi Realty, and Prestige Estates on one side; Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, and Indus Towers on the other. Both sectors are highly sensitive to interest rates, both carry heavy debt, and both have metrics that most retail investors never look at. This lesson gives you those metrics.
Real Estate: Why Revenue Tells You About the Past

markDefs.definition: The total value of homes booked by customers during a period, also called bookings. It is a sales measure, not an accounting revenue figure, and is usually reported in crores and in million square feet.

children.text: Under current Indian accounting rules, a residential developer generally recognises revenue only when a project is complete and possession is handed over, not when a customer books a flat. Since a project can take three to five years, this year's reported revenue mostly reflects homes sold years ago. To see the business as it is today, investors track
and collections, the cash actually received from customers as construction progresses.

body.title: Value the Bookings
body.prompt: A developer reports that it booked 3 million square feet of residential space during the year at an average realisation of ₹9,000 per square foot. What is its pre-sales value for the year, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: 30,00,000 square feet × ₹9,000 = ₹2,700 crore. Note that this number will not appear in the profit and loss statement for years. Also watch the two components separately: area sold shows volume demand, while realisation per square foot shows pricing power and the shift toward premium projects. A developer can report higher pre-sales value on lower volumes simply by selling costlier homes.

body.caption: The Real Estate Metrics That Matter

cells: Value rising only because of price, with volumes falling
Collections lagging pre-sales, suggesting slow construction or buyer stress
Net debt and net debt to operating cash flow
Whether growth is funded by customers or lenders
How long it would take to clear completed and ongoing stock
Inventory of finished, unsold units piling up
Aggressive land buying at cycle peaks using debt
When revenue and profit will finally be booked
Repeated delays, which also carry RERA consequences

body.text: Indian real estate went through a long downturn after 2013, worsened when funding from housing finance companies and NBFCs dried up in 2018. Weak developers could not complete projects, and buyers shifted decisively toward large, listed, branded developers with the balance sheet to deliver. Consolidation helped the listed names, but the cycle also showed how quickly a leveraged developer can get into trouble when sales slow and funding tightens.

body.title: REITs: the rental side of real estate

children.text: A Real Estate Investment Trust owns income-producing property, mainly office parks and malls in India, and distributes most of its rental cash flow to unitholders. SEBI rules require REITs to distribute a large majority of their distributable cash flow, which makes them behave more like an income instrument than a developer stock. The metrics are completely different from a developer: occupancy rate, rental income, releasing spreads on expiring leases, weighted average lease expiry, net operating income, and distribution yield.

Office REITs depend on corporate demand for space, which is why work-from-home trends, global technology hiring, and leasing by global capability centres matter to them. Retail REITs depend on consumption and mall footfalls. In both, rising interest rates hurt twice: financing costs go up, and the yield investors demand rises, which pushes unit prices down.

body.title: Record Pre-Sales, Rising Debt
body.scenario: A listed developer announces record annual pre-sales of ₹9,000 crore, up 30%. In the same results: collections were ₹6,200 crore, construction and land spending was ₹7,800 crore, net debt rose from ₹3,400 crore to ₹5,100 crore, and the company acquired three new land parcels. Reported revenue fell 12% because fewer projects reached completion this year. The stock falls 6% on the revenue decline.
body.prompt: How would you read this set of numbers?
body.modelAnswer: The revenue fall is largely an accounting artefact of completion timing and says little about current demand; record pre-sales say much more. The real question is funding. Collections of ₹6,200 crore against ₹7,800 crore of construction and land spending means the business consumed cash this year, and net debt rose by ₹1,700 crore to fund it. That is acceptable if the land bought will generate profitable launches, but it is exactly how developers got into trouble in the last downcycle. Look at: the gap between pre-sales and collections, and whether construction is on schedule; how much of the spending was land acquisition versus construction; net debt to operating cash flow and the cost of that debt; the expected launch timeline and pricing for new land; unsold inventory in completed projects; and when the current pre-sales will convert into reported revenue and profit. If pre-sales stay strong and collections catch up, the debt is a growth investment. If sales slow while land payments continue, leverage becomes the problem.

children.text: Telecom: A Fixed-Cost Network and One Number Called ARPU

A telecom operator builds towers, lays fibre, buys spectrum in government auctions, and then sells access to that network. Once the network exists, carrying more data costs very little, so almost every extra rupee of revenue flows to operating profit. The headline metric is average revenue per user per month, or ARPU, multiplied by the subscriber base. Because Indian tariffs are among the lowest in the world, small ARPU increases translate into very large profit changes.

body.latex: \text{Monthly revenue} = \text{ARPU} \times \text{Subscribers} \qquad \text{Annual revenue impact of a tariff hike} = \Delta\text{ARPU} \times \text{Subscribers} \times 12
body.caption: With a largely fixed cost network, most of a tariff-driven revenue increase flows through to EBITDA

body.title: What a ₹20 ARPU Increase Is Worth
body.prompt: A telecom operator has 40 crore subscribers and raises ARPU from ₹180 to ₹200 a month, with no subscriber losses. How much additional revenue does this generate in a year, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Extra revenue per month = ₹20 × 40 crore subscribers = ₹800 crore. Over 12 months, that is ₹9,600 crore. Since network costs barely change, the bulk of this flows to EBITDA, which is why telecom stocks react so strongly to tariff hikes. In practice some subscribers downgrade or leave, so watch subscriber numbers alongside ARPU.

body.title: Illustrative Telecom Operator: ARPU and EBITDA Margin

children.text: The other half of telecom is capital. Spectrum bought at auction is paid for over years and amortised, networks need constant upgrading, and each technology shift, from 4G to 5G and beyond, demands a fresh capital cycle before any revenue arrives. Add the industry's history of regulatory dues, and you get a sector where balance sheet strength decides survival. India's mobile market has consolidated into a small number of private operators plus a state-owned player, and that structure is exactly why tariff increases have become possible at all.

body.title: Which Signal Matters Most?
body.question: A telecom operator reports flat revenue for the quarter. Which additional disclosure would most change your view of the business?
options: Its advertising spend fell this quarter
ARPU rose 8% while the subscriber base shrank 7%, with losses concentrated in low-usage second SIM users
It opened new retail stores in three cities
Its depreciation charge rose because of new network assets
body.explanation: The mix inside flat revenue matters enormously. Rising ARPU with losses among low-value users can mean a healthier, more profitable subscriber base, since those users contributed little revenue but some cost. If the losses were among high-value users, the same flat revenue would be a serious warning. The other disclosures are minor or expected consequences of investment.

body.text: Both sectors reward patience with the numbers. In real estate, cash flow and pre-sales lead reported profit by years. In telecom, capital spending leads revenue by years. In each case, the investor who tracks the leading measure sees the turn well before the profit and loss statement shows it.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: Because developers recognise revenue only on project completion, investors track ___ and collections to judge current demand.
body.explanation: Pre-sales capture what customers are booking now, while reported revenue reflects projects sold years earlier.

body.title: Analysing a Developer or a Telecom Operator
steps: For developers, start with pre-sales value and area sold, then compare with collections for the same period
Check operating cash flow after construction and land spending, and the change in net debt
Review unsold inventory, project delivery timelines, and the launch pipeline
Ignore short-term swings in reported revenue caused by completion timing, but note when large projects will be handed over
For telecom, track ARPU, subscriber additions or losses, and data usage per user together
Check capex to revenue, spectrum and regulatory liabilities, and net debt to EBITDA
In both sectors, test how earnings and debt servicing would look if interest rates rose by two percentage points

points: Residential developers recognise revenue on project completion, so reported revenue reflects sales made years earlier
Pre-sales, collections, operating cash flow, and net debt are the real-time measures of a developer's health
Watch pre-sales volume and realisation separately, since value can rise on price alone
REITs are a different business: rental income, occupancy, lease expiries, and distribution yield, and they are sensitive to interest rates
Telecom is a fixed-cost network business, so ARPU increases flow largely to EBITDA and small tariff hikes move profits sharply
Telecom requires repeated capital cycles for spectrum and technology upgrades, so balance sheet strength decides who survives
Both sectors are capital heavy and rate sensitive; leading indicators move well before reported profit

body.text: Pre-sales, ARPU, subscriber, and margin figures in this lesson are illustrative and do not represent any specific company. Accounting and regulatory rules change; refer to company disclosures, SEBI REIT regulations, and TRAI data for current information.
